reader.title: Lynching of Donaldson (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob took Donaldson out of jail and hanged him (A5).

The only report says a mob took Donaldson, called a desperado, out of jail and hanged him, a killing by a group without lawful authority against a man held in custody, which carries the pretext of punishing him (A5). The report is a single, partly illegible editorial item that gives no date, accusation or race.
Only the Brenham Weekly Banner item, itself relaying a Jefferson Democrat correspondent, reports the hanging (A5); the Dangerfield briefs do not mention Donaldson or a jail seizure (A1, A2).

summary.text: The lynching of Donaldson was the hanging of a man described as a "desperado," whom a mob took out of the jail at a town printed as "Dainfield" in 1881.
The only known report, a brief editorial item in the Brenham Weekly Banner of September 15, 1881, gave no date, charge or race for the victim.
The item drew notice for a local correspondent's claim that the town's people regretted the violence, which the Banner answered with skepticism.
The coverage says nothing of Donaldson's alleged offense or how long he had been held, beyond calling him a "desperado."
Early in September, news briefs reported that a gang of desperadoes had committed "lawless acts" in Dangerfield and other Texas towns and that pursuing citizens had killed one of them.
No article connects Donaldson with that gang, and none says whether "Dainfield" and Dangerfield were the same place.
According to the Banner, "A mob took Donaldson, a [des]perado, out of jail at Dainfield and hung him."
The item names no members of the mob, gives no size for it, and does not say where or at what hour the hanging took place.
A correspondent of the Jefferson Democrat, writing from the town, said its people regretted the violence and opposed mob law "in every shape."
A garbled clause in the same passage may say they had wanted to see the desperado, or the mob, punished.
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.
The episode survives in a single Texas weekly, which relayed the Jefferson Democrat's correspondent rather than printing a dispatch of its own.
The Banner labeled Donaldson a "desperado" and called the town's disavowal "all very well," adding that opposition to mob law would not restore him to life.
It then turned to juries and the workings of the law, but the rest of the column is too damaged to read, so its final position on the hanging cannot be determined.
The item uses no racial terms, and no other paper's account of the hanging was found.
